4609.heading: Regression Reference Group
4609.content:
A regression reference group is the category against which indicator-variable coefficients are interpreted. Its observations receive zero on every indicator representing the other levels of the same categorical variable.

Choosing a plausible low-risk or otherwise meaningful group can make coefficients easier to explain. Unknown values sometimes remain in the reference group for practical reasons, but doing so changes its meaning and should be disclosed in the model presentation.

The source shows that R's design matrix omits one factor level and places its fitted mean in the intercept. Coefficients for the remaining levels then represent differences from this reference, so changing the reference changes individual coefficient meanings without changing the fitted group means.

4618.content:
A regression interaction term represents a relationship in which the effect of one explanatory variable depends on the level of another. It is commonly formed as a product while retaining the corresponding lower-order terms.

Once an interaction is included, the lower-order coefficients cannot be interpreted as universal effects. Estimates become stratum-specific combinations of coefficients, so unplanned interaction searches can both inflate false positives and make the model difficult to communicate.

The source constructs interaction columns by multiplying existing design-matrix columns. In R formula syntax, `type:leg` adds only the product terms, while `type*leg` expands to both main effects and their interaction.

4621.content:
The regression F-statistic compares the variability explained by a linear model with its unexplained variability, accounting for their degrees of freedom. Its p-value tests whether the included slope coefficients are jointly zero under the model assumptions.

A significant overall F-test does not imply that every predictor is important or that the model fits well in an absolute sense. Individual coefficients, residual diagnostics, and the size of explained variation remain necessary.

4624.title: Regression Collinearity
4624.heading: Regression Collinearity
4624.content:
Regression collinearity occurs when explanatory variables carry overlapping information. Their conditional coefficients and p-values can become unstable because the model has difficulty separating their individual contributions.

The symptom may appear when a covariate loses or regains significance as related terms enter the model. Thoughtful variable design, correlation review, and a second selection round can reduce redundancy, but a large sample does not automatically eliminate collinearity.

The source diagnoses exact collinearity when a design matrix has fewer independent columns than model terms. In that case, multiple coefficient vectors produce the same fitted values, so an intended effect is not uniquely estimable regardless of the fitting algorithm.

4627.title: Registration Uncertainty
4627.heading: Registration Uncertainty
4627.content:
Registration uncertainty is the range of plausible locations for an augmentation when tracking, calibration, or the world model is imperfect. Presenting one exact position can falsely imply more certainty than the system possesses.

A visualization can encode uncertainty through a region, altered appearance, or another visual cue. The representation should help the user distinguish imprecise placement from the physical extent of the underlying object.

4636.title: Refresh Rate
4636.heading: Refresh Rate
4636.content:
Refresh rate is the frequency with which an [[Output Device]] updates what it presents, usually measured in hertz.

For a [[Visual Display]], refresh rate is how quickly the device refreshes the image from the frame buffer. It is distinct from frame rate, which is how quickly the graphics system generates frames. Low visual refresh rates can cause flicker, while higher rates can help reduce [[Latency]].

For a [[Haptic Display]], temporal resolution is often described as refresh rate. Force feedback requires rapid updates; insufficient temporal resolution can create unintended vibration and make virtual objects feel softer than intended.

Display refresh places a lower bound on when a completed AR image can become visible. A nominal 60-hertz display offers a frame interval of about 17 milliseconds, but sensing, processing, rendering, and scanout add their own delay to the complete motion-to-display path.

4639.title: Reflective Scoring
4639.heading: Reflective Scoring
4639.content:
Reflective scoring describes a player's pattern of choices without ranking one pattern as universally better. Several measures can show tendencies such as directness, restraint, independence, or collaboration rather than collapsing the experience into one high-to-low scale.

This form of [[Game Score|score]] turns evaluation into a mirror. It encourages the player to consider the style of performance created through cumulative decisions instead of optimizing toward a single approved result.

4642.title: Reflective Choice
4642.heading: Reflective Choice
4642.content:
A reflective choice asks the player to consider values, identity, or attitude even though the selected option does not change the plot or game state. Its purpose is to focus attention on the act of choosing and on what that choice means to the player.

Because meaning can arise from interpretation rather than only from mechanical consequence, a reflective choice may affect the experience without altering the outcome. It can ask who the player or character is within the story when no decision can produce a perfect result.

4645.title: Reflection Consistency
4645.heading: Reflection Consistency
4645.content:
Reflection consistency checks whether an object and its image in a mirror or other planar reflective surface obey the geometry of reflection. Corresponding points should be related by a common mirror plane, and the reflected scene should preserve the appropriate reversed viewpoint.

A composite may place a plausible-looking duplicate in the mirror without satisfying those shared constraints. Reliable use requires identifying the reflective plane and corresponding features; curved, warped, or imperfect surfaces demand a different model.

4651.title: Referential Transparency
4651.heading: Referential Transparency
4651.content: An expression is referentially transparent when replacing it with its evaluated value leaves the program's observable behavior unchanged. A pure price calculation has this property for fixed inputs; a call that reads a changing database or prints a message does not. This substitution view makes it easier to compose calculations and reason about them independently of execution order.

4654.title: Reference Map
4654.heading: Reference Map
4654.content: A reference map helps locate named geographic features such as roads, settlements, boundaries, and landmarks. Its purpose is orientation rather than emphasizing one statistical variable. Web tiles can supply this context beneath a thematic layer, provided the thematic data are transformed to the tile system. Excess detail competes with symbols, so reference content should be selected according to scale and the locations readers need to recognize.

4657.title: Rees Algebra
4657.heading: Rees Algebra
4657.content:
The Rees algebra of an ideal I is R(I) = ⊕_{n≥0} Iⁿtⁿ inside R[t]. It packages every power of I into one [[Graded Ring]] while retaining multiplication among the powers.

Quotienting by the ideal generated by t in the appropriate presentation yields the [[Associated Graded Ring]]. Rees algebras connect filtrations, blowup-style geometry, and implicit equations.

4663.title: Reference Frame
4663.heading: Reference Frame
4663.content:
A reference frame establishes what positions, orientations, and movements are measured relative to.

An egocentric frame is relative to the user's body, such as the eyes, head, torso, hands, or legs, and corresponds to a first-person view. An exocentric frame is relative to an object or the world and corresponds to an outside or third-person view.

In a [[3D User Interface]], changing between egocentric and exocentric views can help different tasks but may also confuse the user. [[Navigation]], [[System Control]], and [[3D Manipulation]] should use a frame that makes their mappings easy to predict.

4666.title: Redux
4666.heading: Redux
4666.content:
Redux is a library for coordinating application state through a single store and a constrained update process. Components read selected state and request changes by dispatching actions rather than modifying shared values directly.

Its predictable data flow helps when state must be shared across distant React components. The added structure is most useful when local component state no longer expresses the application's relationships clearly.

4669.title: Redux Thunk
4669.heading: Redux Thunk
4669.content:
Redux Thunk is middleware that lets dispatch accept a function in addition to a plain action object. That function receives dispatch and can perform asynchronous work before sending ordinary actions to the reducer.

In an API workflow, a thunk can dispatch a request action, await the response, and then dispatch either success or failure. The reducer remains synchronous even though the wider operation spans time.

4672.title: Redux Store
4672.heading: Redux Store
4672.content:
A Redux store holds the application's shared state tree and coordinates access to it. It exposes the current state, accepts dispatched actions, and notifies subscribers after the reducer has produced a new state.

The store is the meeting point between action-producing code and state-consuming UI. React components normally receive it through a provider instead of importing a mutable global value.

4675.title: Redux State
4675.heading: Redux State
4675.content:
Redux state is the read-only snapshot of shared application data held by the store. Code does not edit that snapshot in place; it dispatches an action and lets a reducer calculate the replacement state.

This constraint makes each transition traceable to a particular action. Components can select only the portion they need while the store retains one coherent source of truth.

4678.title: Redux Reducer
4678.heading: Redux Reducer
4678.content:
A Redux reducer is a pure function that receives the current state and an action and returns the next state. It expresses how each recognized event transforms the store without mutating the existing state object.

Keeping reducers deterministic makes state changes easier to reason about and test. An unrecognized action returns the current state, preserving the store when no transition applies.

4681.title: Redux Provider
4681.heading: Redux Provider
4681.content:
A Redux provider places the store into React's component context so descendants can access it without passing the store through every intermediate prop. It normally wraps the application near the root of the component tree.

The provider supplies access, while connected components or hooks choose which state and dispatch operations they consume. This keeps the store shared without making every component depend on its entire contents.

4684.title: Redux Action
4684.heading: Redux Action
4684.content:
A Redux action is an object that describes an event that may change application state. Its type identifies what happened, and additional fields carry the data the reducer needs to interpret that event.

Actions describe requested transitions without performing them. Dispatching the action sends it through the store to the reducer, which decides the resulting state.

4687.title: Redux Dispatch
4687.heading: Redux Dispatch
4687.content:
Redux dispatch is the store operation that submits an action for processing. The store passes the action and current state to the reducer, installs the returned state, and makes the update visible to subscribers.

Components dispatch events instead of directly changing shared state. This creates one observable route through which application-wide transitions occur.

4689.title: Redux Action Creator
4689.heading: Document

4690.sourceSearchName: redux action creator redux action creator
4690.title: Redux Action Creator
4690.heading: Redux Action Creator
4690.content:
A Redux action creator is a function that constructs an action. Centralizing this construction gives calling code a stable operation and keeps action types and payload shapes from being repeated throughout components.

A synchronous action creator returns an action immediately. With middleware such as Redux Thunk, an action creator can instead coordinate asynchronous work and dispatch later actions as that work progresses.

4699.title: Reductionism
4699.heading: Reductionism
4699.content:
Reductionism explains something by dividing it into smaller parts and analyzing those parts. This analytic move is valuable for identifying attributes, state, and mechanisms.

Taken too far, reductionism ignores how parts interact and can therefore miss [[Feedback Loop|feedback loops]] and [[Emergence|emergent]] properties. [[Systems Thinking]] retains part-level analysis while recombining it with [[Holism|holistic]] attention to the operating whole.

A recursively enumerable language can be listed by a machine that runs indefinitely, eventually outputting every member and no nonmember. The order need not be fixed, and repetitions are allowed.

This class is equivalent to the [[Turing-Acceptable Language|Turing-acceptable languages]], the ranges of Turing-computable enumerating functions, and the languages generated by general grammars. 4717.title: Recursive Language
4717.heading: Recursive Language
4717.content:
A recursive language is a synonym for a [[Turing-Decidable Language]]. Membership is determined by a computation that always halts with either acceptance or rejection.

A language is recursive exactly when both it and its complement are [[Recursively Enumerable Language|recursively enumerable]]. Running their accepting machines in alternating steps guarantees that one halts and reveals the correct decision for each input.

4723.title: Recursive Definition
4723.heading: Recursive Definition
4723.content:
A recursive definition specifies initial values and then defines later or larger objects in terms of earlier or smaller ones. The factorial definition fixes 0! = 1 and defines n! = n(n − 1)! for n > 0; the Fibonacci sequence requires two initial values before applying its recurrence.

Because the definition builds an infinite family from finite rules, facts about recursively defined objects are commonly proved with [[Mathematical Induction]] or [[Strong Induction]].

The proof also reveals the termination structure: every recursive call must move toward a base case. [[Strong Induction]] is especially useful when a call operates on substructures whose sizes can be any value below the original size.

4732.title: Recurrent Weight Sharing Across Time
4732.heading: Recurrent Weight Sharing Across Time
4732.content:
An [[Recurrent Neural Network]] applies the same recurrent connection weights at each step of a sequence. When the network is [[Time-Unrolled Recurrent Network|unrolled]], the arrows between successive hidden states depict repeated uses of one parameter set, not new parameters for each time position.

This allows a sequence-processing rule to be reused regardless of the step being processed. It also creates a training difficulty: a gradient traveling through many steps repeatedly passes through transformations involving the same weights. The book explains that repeated multiplication by factors below one can make an early-step gradient shrink sharply.

4735.title: Recurrent Neural Network
4735.heading: Recurrent Neural Network
4735.content:
A recurrent neural network processes a sequence while carrying information from earlier steps into later ones. Its recurrent connections make the current output depend on both the present input and a representation of prior inputs.

This structure fits speech and language, where word or sound interpretation depends on surrounding sequence context. [[Long Short-Term Memory]] units were developed to preserve relevant information across longer spans.

Kelleher depicts the network's [[Recurrent Hidden State|hidden state]] as a memory buffer whose activations are fed into the next step along with its new input. [[Time-Unrolled Recurrent Network|Unrolling]] the loop shows how one set of [[Recurrent Weight Sharing Across Time|shared recurrent weights]] is reused through a sequence. Training with [[Backpropagation Through Time]] then has to propagate error through those steps, which can make long-range dependencies difficult to learn.

4738.title: Recurrent Hidden State
4738.heading: Recurrent Hidden State
4738.content:
A recurrent network carries a vector of hidden-layer activations from one sequence step into the next. At the current step, the hidden layer receives both the new input and this stored context. Its output is used to produce the current result and to update the state for the following step.

The memory buffer in Kelleher's [[Recurrent Neural Network]] diagram stores activations without transforming them; weighted connections from the buffer to the hidden units perform the next transformation. This feedback lets a later input be processed in the context of earlier inputs, although basic recurrence can struggle to retain long-range information during training.

4741.sourceSearchName: rectifier activation function rectifier activation function
4741.title: Rectifier Activation Function
4741.heading: Rectifier Activation Function
4741.content:
The rectifier activation function maps every negative input to zero and returns positive input in direct proportion to its value. A neuron using this function is called a rectified linear unit, or ReLU.

Unlike sigmoid and tanh, the positive side does not flatten toward a fixed maximum. Different neural architectures favor different [[Activation Function|activation functions]], and ReLU units are common building blocks in deep networks.

Kelleher emphasizes the training tradeoff: the rectifier's derivative is one on its positive side, letting gradients pass through active units without the repeated shrinkage of a saturated sigmoid. Its negative side has zero gradient, however, so inactive units do not train from that local signal. A leaky variant introduces a nonzero negative-side slope. The activation choice affects both representational behavior and the [[Vanishing Gradient Problem|flow of training gradients]].

4744.title: Rectangular Matrix
4744.heading: Rectangular Matrix
4744.content:
A rectangular matrix has a different number of rows and columns. An $m\times n$ matrix is rectangular when $m\neq n$.

Rectangular coefficient matrices naturally describe [[Overdetermined Linear System|overdetermined]] and [[Underdetermined Linear System|underdetermined]] systems. They do not have ordinary two-sided inverses, but a [[Pseudoinverse]] and [[Least Squares Approximation]] can supply useful generalized solutions.

4747.content:
Rectangular fin parameterization defines length, width, thickness, base dimensions, and relevant offsets as named quantities rather than fixed sketch coordinates. A profile and block can then be rebuilt consistently when any dimension changes.

The parameterized construction supports one-, two-, and three-dimensional comparisons and systematic sweeps. Derived measurements such as tip area, perimeter, and volume provide checks that the rebuilt geometry matches the intended proportions.

Applying these rules determines the population to which results can be generalized. Criteria should be decided before model fitting, expressed in executable code, and paired with counts so the effect of every filtering step remains visible.

4759.heading: Record Exclusion Audit
4759.content:
A record exclusion audit preserves or counts observations removed by each filtering rule. Instead of viewing exclusion as a silent side effect, the analyst records why rows left the analysis and how many were affected.

The audit can reveal selection bias, especially when a required measure is missing for most people with the outcome. It also supports rollback and verification by showing that retained and excluded partitions reconcile with the input dataset.

Removing observations with a missing target is a consequential modeling decision in the book's preparation workflow. Recording the affected rows and counts distinguishes a justified analytic population from an accidental loss of data.

4762.title: Reconverging Branches
4762.heading: Reconverging Branches
4762.content:
Reconverging branches are narrative paths that separate after a choice and later return to a shared plot line. They preserve some variation in the journey while limiting the amount of permanently divergent material a [[Branching Story]] requires.

Reconvergence can support different details, perspectives, or routes to one outcome. If branches return without acknowledging meaningful differences, however, the earlier choice may feel unsupported or merely cosmetic.

4765.title: Reciprocal
4765.heading: Reciprocal
4765.content:
The reciprocal of a nonzero number is the value that multiplies with it to produce the multiplicative [[Identity Element]] one. For a nonzero fraction,

$$\left(\frac{c}{d}\right)^{-1}=\frac{d}{c}.$$

Thus the reciprocal of (3/5) is (5/3). Division by a nonzero fraction is multiplication by its reciprocal:

$$\frac{a}{b}\div\frac{c}{d}=\frac{a}{b}\cdot\frac{d}{c}.$$

Zero has no reciprocal because no number multiplied by zero equals one.

4768.title: Recommender System
4768.heading: Recommender System
4768.content:
A recommender system predicts or ranks items that may be useful to a user from observed preferences, item information, or interactions. Its output reduces a large choice space to a personalized set of candidates.

Different systems rely on [[Collaborative Filtering]], [[Content-Based Recommendation]], or a hybrid. The appropriate design depends on available feedback, scale, changing context, and how recommendation quality will be evaluated.

4771.heading: Reciprocal Conversion Factors
4771.content: A factor for one direction of a compatible conversion can be inverted for the reverse direction. Pryor's fuel-efficiency example uses a kilometers-per-mile ratio in the numerator but the reciprocal of liters-per-gallon in the denominator, so gallons cancel and liters remain below kilometers. Bidirectional conversion still requires choosing the correct orientation for each unit appearing in a compound expression. A reciprocal does not by itself handle scales with an offset, such as absolute Fahrenheit and Celsius readings. See [[Temperature Readings versus Intervals]].

4774.title: Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve
4774.heading: Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve
4774.content:
A receiver operating characteristic curve plots true-positive rate against false-positive rate as the decision threshold of a probabilistic binary classifier varies. Each point represents a different discrete operating rule.

Curves toward the upper-left indicate stronger separation, and the area under the curve summarizes ranking performance across thresholds. Operational selection still requires a specific balance between missed positives and false alarms.

The book uses ROC curves to compare predictive models across possible probability cutoffs rather than fixing one threshold prematurely. It pairs the curve with area under the curve and risk-oriented displays that connect ranking quality to use.

4777.title: Receiver Clock Bias
4777.heading: Receiver Clock Bias
4777.content: Receiver clock bias is the offset between a navigation receiver's local clock and the satellite-system time scale. The offset adds nearly the same apparent range error to all simultaneously observed satellites, because electromagnetic signals travel about 300 meters in one microsecond. Rather than equipping every receiver with an atomic clock, GPS includes clock bias in the navigation equations and estimates it from an additional satellite measurement.

4780.heading: Real-Virtual Consistency
4780.content:
Real-virtual consistency is the requirement that software state remain compatible with the physical objects and processes it represents. A real object may move, appear, disappear, or be changed by a person outside the application's control.

The AR system must sense relevant changes and update virtual behavior without violating expected physical relationships. This consistency extends beyond appearance to interaction, semantics, timing, and the consequences of acting on real objects.

4783.title: Recall
4783.heading: Recall
4783.content:
Recall is the proportion of actual positive cases that a classifier identifies. It is also called sensitivity or the true-positive rate and falls when false negatives increase.

Thresholds that raise recall often lower [[Precision]], making the tradeoff a decision question rather than a purely technical optimum.

4786.title: Real-Time Stream Processing
4786.heading: Real-Time Stream Processing
4786.content:
Real-time stream processing analyzes events while they are arriving so results can influence a situation before their value expires. Operators maintain bounded state, transform records, detect patterns, and emit alerts or updates without waiting for a complete dataset.

IoT streams intensify the problem through many geographically distributed producers, high rates, diverse formats, and limited device resources.

4789.title: Real-Time State Synchronization
4789.heading: Real-Time State Synchronization
4789.content:
Real-time state synchronization maps a received server event into the client state that drives the interface. A SignalR handler can append or replace the relevant value so React rerenders without a manual refresh.

The event payload and state transition must agree on identity and ordering. The live message improves freshness, while a later authoritative fetch can restore consistency after a missed or interrupted connection.

In a networked game, synchronization also depends on topology. A client-server model distributes authoritative updates from one server, while peer-to-peer simulations may exchange commands and require each machine to advance deterministic state in the same order.

4792.content:
Real-time global illumination approximates light that travels through multiple surface interactions quickly enough for an interactive display. In AR, it can support diffuse color transfer, indirect shadows, and specular effects connecting real and virtual objects.

The method must update as the viewpoint, objects, or lights change, while respecting a strict frame budget. Practical techniques trade physical completeness for an approximation whose most visible common-lighting effects remain coherent.

4801.title: Real Number
4801.heading: Real Number
4801.content:
A real number is any [[Rational Number]] or [[Irrational Number]]. The real numbers fill the [[Number Line]]: each point corresponds to a real value, and order corresponds to position from left to right.

Elementary algebra generally treats variables as real unless another domain is specified. The real-number system supports addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division by nonzero values, along with order comparisons. Restrictions still matter; for example, a denominator cannot equal zero, and an even root is not a real number when its radicand is negative.

4819.title: Reactive System
4819.heading: Reactive System
4819.content: A reactive system is an architectural arrangement designed to remain responsive under changing load and partial failure. The book describes responsiveness, scalability, resilience, and message-based communication as its related properties. This is broader than using an observable sequence inside one process: component boundaries, resource allocation, and failure isolation determine whether the whole service can keep responding.

4822.title: Reactive Stream
4822.heading: Reactive Stream
4822.content: A reactive stream is a time-ordered sequence of notifications. It may emit values, report an error, and signal completion, so a consumer must consider more than the next ordinary value. User events, inventory updates, and calculated totals can each be treated as streams. Operators can derive new streams without requiring producers to know every downstream consumer.

4825.title: Reactive Stream Merge
4825.heading: Reactive Stream Merge
4825.content: Merging reactive streams forms one output sequence from notifications arriving on several input sequences. The book combines two ticket-counter streams so one observer can consume both. The resulting interleaving follows arrival and scheduling rather than a guaranteed sorted order, so a consumer that needs global ordering must establish that separately.

4828.heading: Reactive Stream Filtering
4828.content: Filtering a reactive stream forwards only notifications whose values satisfy a predicate. The book applies a threshold to a merged number stream, leaving the original producers unchanged while the downstream observer sees a smaller sequence. This turns a selection rule into a composable stage of event processing rather than a condition embedded in every producer.

4831.title: Reactive Programming
4831.heading: Reactive Programming
4831.content: Reactive programming models changing values as asynchronous streams and expresses what should happen when new values arrive. Rather than repeatedly asking whether a quantity changed, a consumer subscribes to notifications and transforms the resulting sequence. The book's inventory examples use observable product updates and stream operations to separate producers from the code that responds to them.

4834.content: Mapping a reactive stream transforms each emitted value into a value for a derived stream. In the book's numerical example, a stage adds three to each value after merging and filtering. 4837.content: Reactive Extensions, commonly called Rx, provide operators and supporting types for composing .NET observable sequences. 4840.title: Reactive Assistant
4840.heading: Reactive Assistant
4840.content:
A reactive assistant acts in response to an explicit user request or event. The user initiates the exchange, so the immediate purpose of the interaction is comparatively clear.

Reactive behavior limits interruption and privacy risks, but it cannot surface useful information before the user thinks to ask. A [[Proactive Assistant]] takes the stronger step of initiating an interaction.

4843.title: React
4843.heading: React
4843.content:
React is an open-source JavaScript library for building component-based browser interfaces. A React application expresses the visible interface as a tree of elements produced by components and rerenders affected output when component state changes.

React supplies the component and rendering model rather than a complete full-stack framework. Libraries such as [[React Router]] and [[Redux]] add routing and shared state, while an ASP.NET Core [[Web API]] can provide the back end.

4846.title: React useState Hook
4846.heading: React useState Hook
4846.content:
The React `useState` hook adds one piece of local state to a function component. It returns the current value and a setter function, while its argument supplies the initial value.

Calling the setter schedules a rerender with the new state. TypeScript can infer the state type from the initial value or accept an explicit generic type when values such as `null` and loaded data are both possible.

4849.title: React useEffect Hook
4849.heading: React useEffect Hook
4849.content:
The React `useEffect` hook performs a side effect after a function component renders. Fetching data, starting a subscription, or responding to a changed route parameter are effects because they reach beyond calculation of the returned element tree.

Its dependency array controls when the effect is repeated. An empty array runs the effect after the initial render, while listed values cause it to rerun when one changes. Cleanup can stop work when the component is removed.

4852.title: React Router
4852.heading: React Router
4852.content:
React Router is a client-side routing library that maps browser locations to React components. It lets a single-page application present multiple navigable pages without requesting a complete HTML document for each route.

Routes can redirect, select a not-found component, capture path parameters, and load components lazily. Link and history APIs change location while keeping navigation inside the client application.

4855.title: React Rendering
4855.heading: React Rendering
4855.content:
React rendering evaluates a component to produce the element tree for its current props and state. A state change rerenders the component and ordinarily its children so React can update the browser output.

Rerendering is not identical to replacing the entire document. React applies the required changes, and memoization can prevent an unchanged child from being evaluated unnecessarily when its props remain equivalent.

4858.title: React Link
4858.heading: React Link
4858.content:
A React Router Link renders navigable content that changes the client-side location without forcing a full document request. It preserves browser navigation behavior while letting the router select the destination component.

Links are appropriate when navigation is part of rendered content. An event handler that decides a destination after work completes can use [[Programmatic Navigation]] instead.

4861.title: React Form
4861.heading: React Form
4861.content:
A React form coordinates controlled field values, validation state, submission progress, and success or failure behavior. The browser form event is handled by component logic so the application can validate and send data without an automatic page navigation.

Reusable form and field components reduce repeated state and event code. Server-side validation remains necessary even when the React form provides complete client feedback.

4864.title: React Event Handling
4864.heading: React Event Handling
4864.content:
React event handling attaches a function to an element event such as a click, input change, blur, or form submission. The handler receives an event object and can update component state or invoke a callback prop.

Handlers are passed as functions rather than executed during rendering. A form submission handler can prevent the browser's default navigation before validating values and starting an asynchronous request.
